sectionTitle: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Reflection of waves (physics only)

specStatements.text: Waves can be reflected at the boundary between two different materials.
Waves can be absorbed or transmitted at the boundary between two different materials.
Students should be able to construct ray diagrams to illustrate the reflection of a wave at a surface.
Students should be able to describe the effects of reflection, transmission and absorption of waves at material interfaces.
Required practical activity 9 (physics only): investigate the reflection of light by different types of surface and the refraction of light by different substances.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 4 and 8.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

concepts.definition: The surface where one material ends and a different material begins, for example air and glass or air and a brick wall. When a wave arrives at a boundary it can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted, and in most real cases all three happen at once in differing proportions.

The process in which a wave arriving at a boundary is sent back into the material it came from, rather than passing into the second material. Reflection happens at a boundary between any two different materials, not only at mirrors.
Reflection from a smooth surface, such as a plane mirror or still water. Parallel incident rays stay parallel after reflecting, so a clear image is formed.

Reflection from a rough surface, such as paper or a painted wall. The surface behaves as many tiny facets pointing in different directions, so parallel incident rays are scattered and no image is seen. The law of reflection still holds at every point.
The process in which the energy carried by a wave is transferred into the energy stores of the material at the boundary, usually the thermal energy store, so the wave itself does not continue.

The process in which a wave passes through the boundary and continues to travel inside the second material. A transmitted wave usually changes speed, and if it meets the boundary at an angle to the normal it also changes direction.

The change in direction of a transmitted wave at a boundary, caused by the change in the speed of the wave as it enters a different material. A wave travelling along the normal changes speed but does not change direction.

The construction line drawn at right angles to the surface at the point where the ray meets it, shown dashed in a ray diagram. Angles of incidence, reflection and refraction are all measured from the normal.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal at the point of incidence.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence. For any surface, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

A drawing showing the surface, the dashed normal at the point of incidence, the incident ray and the reflected ray, each drawn as a straight line with an arrow giving the direction of travel, with both angles marked from the normal.

What happens to a wave depends on the wave and on the two materials meeting at the interface. A matt black surface absorbs most visible light, a silvered surface reflects most of it, clear glass transmits most of it, and soft furnishings absorb much of the sound reaching them.

An investigation in two parts: shining a ray of light from a ray box at different types of surface and observing and measuring the reflected ray, then shining a ray into different transparent substances, such as a rectangular glass block or a perspex block, and tracing the refracted ray.

The technique of drawing round the block or surface, marking the incident and emerging rays with two pencil crosses set well apart, then removing the block and joining the crosses with a ruler so that the path inside the block can be drawn and the angles measured from the normal.

misconceptions.question: At which boundaries can a wave be reflected?
misconceptions.correct: At the boundary between any two different materials, for example air and water or air and concrete.
misconceptions.misconception: Reflection only happens at mirrors or other shiny polished surfaces.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reflection is nearly always introduced using a plane mirror, so students attach the property to the mirror rather than to the boundary.
misconceptions.correction: A clear image needs a smooth surface, but reflection itself does not. Sound echoes from a rough brick wall and light reflects from matt paper; both are reflections at a boundary.

misconceptions.question: Does the law of reflection still apply to a rough surface such as paper?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. At every point the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence; the surface normals simply point in many different directions.
misconceptions.misconception: Rough surfaces scatter light randomly, so the law of reflection does not apply to them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see the scattered result and conclude the rule has broken down, because they picture the surface as flat rather than as many tiny tilted facets.
misconceptions.correction: Draw the rough surface magnified as a set of small flat facets. Each facet obeys the law of reflection with its own normal, and the different facet directions are what scatter the rays.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the energy of a wave that is absorbed at a boundary?
misconceptions.correct: It is transferred from the wave to the energy stores of the absorbing material, usually the thermal energy store, so the material warms up.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy is used up or destroyed, so there is less energy afterwards than there was before.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language such as 'the sound died away' suggests disappearance, and absorption is often taught only as the wave stopping.
misconceptions.correction: Energy is conserved. Absorption is a transfer, not a loss: a black car roof in sunlight and the warm foam in a sound-proofed room are both evidence of where the energy went.

misconceptions.question: When a wave meets a boundary, does exactly one of reflection, absorption and transmission happen?
misconceptions.correct: No. In general all three happen together at a boundary, in proportions that depend on the wave and on the two materials.
misconceptions.misconception: A wave must do one thing only: it is either reflected, or absorbed, or transmitted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook diagrams usually show a single arrow for a single process, and questions often name just one effect, so students treat them as mutually exclusive.
misconceptions.correction: You can see your own faint reflection in a window while also seeing the street through it, and the glass warms slightly. That one boundary is reflecting, transmitting and absorbing at the same time.

misconceptions.question: Why does a transmitted ray of light change direction as it enters a glass block?
misconceptions.correct: Because the light changes speed at the boundary; entering glass it slows down, and if it meets the boundary at an angle to the normal it bends towards the normal.
misconceptions.misconception: The light bends because glass is heavier or denser and physically pushes the ray sideways.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'dense' is used loosely in everyday speech, so students reach for a mechanical push instead of a change of wave speed.
misconceptions.correction: Refraction is a wave speed effect. The part of the wavefront that reaches the glass first slows first, which swings the whole wavefront round and changes the direction of the ray.

misconceptions.question: A ray of light meets a glass block along the normal. What happens to its direction?
misconceptions.correct: It carries straight on without changing direction, although it does slow down inside the glass.
misconceptions.misconception: Light passes straight on through glass without bending, because transparent glass does not change a ray's direction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn 'light bends towards the normal entering glass' as an unconditional fact and apply it even when the angle of incidence is zero.
misconceptions.correction: At an angle of incidence of 0° the whole wavefront reaches the boundary at the same instant, so there is nothing to swing it round. The speed changes but the direction does not.

misconceptions.question: From which line is the angle of incidence measured?
misconceptions.correct: From the normal, the dashed line drawn at 90° to the surface at the point of incidence.
misconceptions.misconception: From the surface itself, because that is the line the ray strikes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The surface is already drawn and obvious, while the normal has to be added by the student, so it feels like an optional extra.
misconceptions.correction: The two angles add up to 90°, so a ray at 30° to a mirror has an angle of incidence of 60°. Draw the dashed normal first and measure everything from it.

misconceptions.question: Where is the normal drawn in a ray diagram?
misconceptions.correct: At right angles to the surface, at the exact point where the incident ray meets it.
misconceptions.misconception: The normal is a dashed line drawn along the surface itself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember only that the normal is dashed, and copy the dashing onto the most prominent line already in the diagram.
misconceptions.correction: 'Normal' means perpendicular. Check every diagram with a set square: the normal must make 90° with the surface at the point of incidence.

misconceptions.question: A ray meets a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 30°. What is the angle of reflection?
misconceptions.correct: 30°, measured from the normal, on the opposite side of the normal to the incident ray.
misconceptions.misconception: 60°, because the angles marked in the diagram must add up to 90°.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students mix the angle measured from the normal with the angle measured from the surface, and subtract from 90° out of habit.
misconceptions.correction: The law of reflection is angle of reflection = angle of incidence, with both measured from the normal, so 30° in gives 30° out.

misconceptions.question: Where should the image be marked on a ray diagram for a plane mirror?
misconceptions.correct: Behind the mirror, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.
misconceptions.misconception: The image sits on the front surface of the mirror, where you see it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reflecting surface is where the light appears to come from, so students place the image on the glass rather than behind it.
misconceptions.correction: Extend the reflected rays backwards as dashed construction lines. They meet behind the mirror, and that meeting point is where the image is.

misconceptions.question: Why does a matt black surface get hotter in sunlight than a shiny silver one?
misconceptions.correct: Because it absorbs most of the light that reaches it, transferring the energy to its thermal energy store, while the silver surface reflects most of it away.
misconceptions.misconception: The black surface reflects more light, and reflecting light is what warms a surface up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'more happening at the surface' with heating, and reflection is the process they can see, so they credit it with the warming.
misconceptions.correction: Reflected energy leaves the surface again and cannot warm it. Only absorbed energy is transferred into the material, which is why solar absorbers are matt black.

misconceptions.question: How does a thick curtain reduce the noise coming from a busy road?
misconceptions.correct: The soft fabric absorbs much of the sound energy, transferring it to the thermal energy store of the curtain.
misconceptions.misconception: The curtain reflects all the sound waves straight back outside.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know a hard wall echoes and assume any barrier works by bouncing sound away, without distinguishing hard surfaces from soft ones.
misconceptions.correction: Hard smooth surfaces reflect sound and produce echoes; soft porous ones absorb it. That is why recording studios are lined with foam and not with tiles.

misconceptions.question: In Required practical activity 9, which quantity must be kept the same when different surfaces are compared?
misconceptions.correct: The angle of incidence of the ray from the ray box, so that only the type of surface is changed.
misconceptions.misconception: The type of surface should be kept the same each time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students confuse the control variable with the independent variable, and the surface is the thing the question tells them to think about.
misconceptions.correction: The surface is the independent variable, the reflected ray is the dependent variable, and the angle of incidence is the control variable that must be held constant.

misconceptions.question: A ray enters a rectangular glass block from air, meeting the surface at an angle to the normal. Which way does it bend?
misconceptions.correct: Towards the normal, because the light slows down as it goes into the glass.
misconceptions.misconception: Away from the normal, because glass makes light spread out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 'towards' and 'away' rules are memorised as a pair and are easily swapped when the direction of travel is not checked.
misconceptions.correction: Slower means towards the normal. Entering glass the ray bends towards the normal; leaving the block back into air it bends away from it, so the emerging ray is parallel to the original one.

mcqs.stem: A sound wave travelling through the air reaches a thick concrete wall. Which statement best describes reflection at this boundary?

options.text: Some of the sound is sent back into the air it originally came from
options.rationale: Reflection at a boundary sends part of the wave back into the first material, and air and concrete are two different materials.

options.text: Reflection cannot occur here, as concrete is not polished
options.rationale: Students who meet reflection only at mirrors treat a shiny surface, rather than a boundary, as the requirement.

options.text: All of the sound must pass on into the concrete and travel through
options.rationale: Treats the three possible effects as exclusive, and picks transmission because the wall is solid and continuous.

options.text: The wall turns the sound into a wave of a much higher frequency
options.rationale: Confuses reflection with a change in the wave itself; frequency is set by the source and is unchanged by reflection.

mcqs.stem: A lamp lights a plane mirror and a sheet of white paper equally. A clear image is seen in the mirror but not in the paper. Why is this?

options.text: The rough paper scatters rays and so breaks the law of reflection
options.rationale: Sees the scattered result and concludes the rule has failed, instead of picturing many tiny facets each obeying it.

options.text: The paper absorbs every ray of light that arrives at it
options.rationale: Over-applies absorption; a sheet that absorbed all the light reaching it would look black rather than white.

options.text: The smooth mirror keeps parallel rays parallel when they reflect
options.rationale: Specular reflection at a smooth surface preserves the pattern of the rays so an image forms, whereas the rough paper scatters them.

options.text: Paper transmits light, but a mirror is unable to transmit
options.rationale: Confuses transmission with scattering, and assumes an opaque sheet of paper lets light straight through.

mcqs.stem: A radio wave meets a thick metal sheet and is absorbed. What happens to the energy that the wave was carrying?

options.text: It is destroyed, so less energy exists than there was before
options.rationale: Everyday phrases such as 'the signal died' suggest that absorbed energy simply disappears.

options.text: It is transferred to the thermal energy store of the metal
options.rationale: Absorption transfers the energy carried by the wave into the energy stores of the material, most often the thermal store.

options.text: It is stored inside the wave until that wave is set free again
options.rationale: Treats the wave as an object that survives absorption and can later be released intact.

options.text: It becomes a reflected wave of exactly the same frequency
options.rationale: Merges two different effects, assuming anything not transmitted must come back out as a reflection.

mcqs.stem: Light from a street lamp shines on a clean window and carries on into the room beyond. Which word describes what the light has done at the glass?

options.text: The light has been absorbed by glass
options.rationale: Confuses transmission with absorption; light absorbed by the glass would never reach the room.

options.text: The light has been reflected away
options.rationale: Picks the effect that is easiest to see at a window, ignoring the light that clearly gets through.

options.text: The light has been fully destroyed
options.rationale: Assumes the wave simply ends at the boundary, which conflicts with the room being lit.

options.text: The light has been transmitted
options.rationale: Transmission is a wave passing through the boundary and continuing to travel inside the second material.

mcqs.stem: A narrow ray of light travels through air and meets the flat surface of a glass block. Which statement about this boundary is correct?

options.text: All the light is transmitted, because the glass is transparent
options.rationale: Reads 'transparent' as 'all light passes', ignoring the faint reflection seen at every glass surface.

options.text: All the light is absorbed, since the glass warms up a little
options.rationale: Notices that a little absorption happens and wrongly scales it up to the whole beam.

options.text: Some light is transmitted into the glass and some is reflected back
options.rationale: In general all three effects occur together, and a faint reflected ray is visible alongside the much brighter transmitted one.

options.text: None of the light gets in until the angle reaches ninety degrees
options.rationale: Invents a threshold angle for entry, muddling the idea with the critical angle met in refraction work.

mcqs.stem: You are drawing a ray diagram for light reflecting from a plane mirror. From which line is the angle of incidence measured?

options.text: From the normal, drawn at right angles to the mirror surface
options.rationale: Angles of incidence and reflection are always measured between the ray and the normal at the point of incidence.

options.text: From the mirror surface, at the point where the ray lands on it
options.rationale: The surface is already drawn and obvious, so it gets used instead of the normal the student must add.

options.text: From the flat surface, along where the ray hits it
options.rationale: Wrong: the angle of incidence is measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface the ray strikes.

options.text: From the bottom edge of the paper the diagram sits on
options.rationale: Uses the page rather than the optical geometry, so the answer would change if the paper were turned.

mcqs.stem: A ray strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 30°. What is the angle of reflection, and from where is it measured?

options.text: 60°, measured from the normal, since they total 90°
options.rationale: Subtracts from 90° out of habit, mixing the angle from the normal with the angle from the surface.

options.text: 30°, measured from the surface of the mirror
options.rationale: Gets the size of the angle right but measures it from the wrong line, so the drawn ray ends up misplaced.

options.text: 60°, measured from the mirror surface, not the normal
options.rationale: Combines both errors: subtracts from 90° and then measures the result from the surface.

options.text: 30°, measured from the normal on its other side
options.rationale: The law of reflection gives angle of reflection = angle of incidence, with both angles measured from the normal.

mcqs.stem: Which feature must appear in a correctly drawn ray diagram showing reflection at a plane mirror?

options.text: A dashed normal drawn along the mirror surface
options.rationale: Remembers that the normal is dashed but puts it on the most prominent line rather than at 90° to the surface.

options.text: Arrows on the rays to show the direction
options.rationale: Rays are drawn as straight lines carrying arrows, so the diagram shows which way the light is travelling.

options.text: The image marked in front of the mirror surface
options.rationale: Places the image where the light appears to come from rather than behind the reflecting surface.

options.text: An angle of reflection larger than incidence
options.rationale: Assumes the ray opens out on reflection, which contradicts the law of reflection.

mcqs.stem: A matt black metal plate and a shiny silver metal plate are left side by side in bright sunlight. Why does the black plate become hotter?

options.text: It reflects more of the light, and reflection is what warms a surface
options.rationale: Credits the visible process with the heating, but reflected energy leaves the surface and cannot warm it.

options.text: The silver plate reflects all the light, so it absorbs none and cannot warm up
options.rationale: Confuses transmission with absorption; an opaque metal plate transmits essentially no light at all.

options.text: The silver plate absorbs the light but re-emits all of it at once
options.rationale: Invents instant re-emission to explain why the shiny plate stays cool, instead of using reflection.

options.text: It absorbs more of the light, transferring that energy to its thermal store
options.rationale: Absorption at the interface transfers the energy of the wave into the material and raises its temperature; reflected energy leaves again.

mcqs.stem: Heavy fabric curtains are drawn across a window facing a busy road, and the room becomes noticeably quieter. Which effect best explains this?

options.text: The curtain reflects all the sound waves straight back
options.rationale: Assumes any barrier works by bouncing sound away, without distinguishing hard surfaces from soft ones.

options.text: The soft fabric absorbs much of the sound that reaches it
options.rationale: Soft porous materials absorb sound, transferring the energy of the wave to their thermal energy store, so less is transmitted into the room.

options.text: The curtain bounces the noise straight back outdoors
options.rationale: Wrong: soft heavy fabric mainly absorbs sound energy; it does not reflect it all back outside.

options.text: The curtain slows the sound so it arrives too late to hear
options.rationale: Confuses a change of speed with a change of loudness; arriving later is not the same as being quieter.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical activity 9 a ray box is aimed at a plane mirror, then at gloss card, then at matt card. Which quantity must be kept the same throughout?

options.text: The angle of incidence of the ray from the box
options.rationale: The type of surface is the independent variable, so the angle of incidence is the control variable and must be held constant.

options.text: The kind of surface that the ray box is aimed at
options.rationale: Names the independent variable, which is the one quantity that is deliberately changed each time.

options.text: The surface type placed in front of the ray box
options.rationale: Wrong: the surface is the independent variable being changed, so it must not be held constant.

options.text: The sharpness of the reflected ray on paper
options.rationale: Names an observation about the reflected ray rather than a variable the student is able to set.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical activity 9 a ray of light is shone from air into a rectangular glass block, meeting the surface at an angle to the normal. What is seen as the ray enters the block?

options.text: It bends away from the normal
options.rationale: Swaps the pair of rules, applying the 'away' case for leaving the block to the ray entering it.

options.text: It carries straight on, unbent
options.rationale: Applies the zero-angle result to a ray that is not travelling along the normal.

options.text: It bends towards the normal
options.rationale: Light slows on entering glass, so a ray meeting the surface at an angle to the normal is refracted towards the normal.

options.text: It spreads out and bends away from the normal
options.rationale: Wrong: entering the denser glass, light bends towards the normal, not away from it.
